history.q: In what year was Nelson Mandela released from prison?
history.fact: Mandela walked free from Victor Verster Prison on 11 February 1990 after 27 years behind bars.

history.q: In what year did South Africa hold its first democratic election open to citizens of all races?
history.fact: Voting began on 27 April 1994, with queues stretching for kilometres; the date is now celebrated as Freedom Day.

history.q: On which island off Cape Town was Nelson Mandela held for 18 of his 27 years in prison?
history.fact: Robben Island became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999, and former political prisoners have guided visitors around it.

history.q: Which Portuguese navigator became the first European to sail around the southern tip of Africa, in 1488?
history.fact: Dias's voyage proved a sea route to the Indian Ocean existed; Vasco da Gama followed it all the way to India a decade later.

history.q: Which trading company set up a supply station at the Cape under Jan van Riebeeck in 1652?
history.fact: The station grew vegetables and traded for cattle to resupply ships sailing between Europe and Asia.

history.q: Which war of 1899-1902 pitted the British Empire against the two Boer republics?
history.fact: Also called the South African War, it was fought against the South African Republic (Transvaal) and the Orange Free State.

history.q: Which king built the Zulu kingdom into a major regional power in the early 19th century?
history.fact: Shaka reorganised Zulu warfare with the short stabbing spear and close formations before his death in 1828.

history.q: Which archbishop won the 1984 Nobel Peace Prize for his nonviolent opposition to apartheid?
history.fact: Tutu popularised the phrase "Rainbow Nation" to describe a South Africa united in its diversity.

history.q: On 16 June 1976, students protesting against Afrikaans as a language of instruction began which uprising?
history.fact: 16 June is now Youth Day, a public holiday honouring the students of 1976.

history.q: In 1960, police killed 69 people at a protest against the pass laws in which township?
history.fact: The massacre took place on 21 March 1960; the date is now marked as Human Rights Day.

history.q: In what year was the Union of South Africa formed from four British colonies?
history.fact: On 31 May 1910 the Cape, Natal, Transvaal and Orange River colonies joined as a self-governing dominion of the British Empire.

history.q: Which 1963-64 trial ended with Nelson Mandela and several co-accused sentenced to life imprisonment?
history.fact: From the dock Mandela declared that a democratic, free society was "an ideal for which I am prepared to die."

history.q: Which founder of the Black Consciousness Movement died in police custody in 1977?
history.fact: Biko's life inspired Peter Gabriel's 1980 song "Biko" and the 1987 film "Cry Freedom."

history.q: Which 1838 battle between Voortrekkers and Zulu forces took place beside the Ncome River?
history.fact: The battle was fought on 16 December, which today is the Day of Reconciliation public holiday.

history.q: At which battle in January 1879 did a Zulu army defeat a British invasion force?
history.fact: Isandlwana was one of the heaviest defeats suffered by a British army against an African force during the colonial era.

history.q: Which 1955 document, adopted at Kliptown, declares that "South Africa belongs to all who live in it, black and white"?
history.fact: Thousands gathered at the Congress of the People in Kliptown, Soweto, on 26 June 1955 to adopt the Charter.

history.q: The discovery of what on the Witwatersrand in 1886 led to the founding of Johannesburg?
history.fact: Johannesburg grew from a mining camp to the country's largest city within a few decades, earning the nickname eGoli, "place of gold."

history.q: From which colony did thousands of Voortrekkers set out on the Great Trek of the 1830s?
history.fact: The trekkers travelled inland by ox wagon, and their journey led to the founding of the Boer republics.

history.q: Which Boer leader was President of the South African Republic (Transvaal) when the Second Boer War began?
history.fact: Kruger later sailed to Europe to seek support; the Kruger National Park and the Krugerrand coin bear his name.

history.q: Which Khoikhoi woman served as an interpreter for Jan van Riebeeck's settlement at the Cape?
history.fact: Krotoa, also called Eva, learned Dutch and Portuguese and became a key go-between in the 1650s.

history.q: Whose prophecies inspired the Xhosa cattle-killing movement of 1856-57?
history.fact: The movement led to a devastating famine in the eastern Cape and greatly weakened Xhosa independence.

history.q: Which Iron Age kingdom flourished near the Limpopo River in the 13th century before Great Zimbabwe rose?
history.fact: A small gold rhinoceros found in a royal grave at Mapungubwe has become a national treasure.

history.q: Which founding leader of the Pan Africanist Congress led the 1960 campaign against the pass laws?
history.fact: After serving his sentence Sobukwe was kept on Robben Island under a law renewed each year, known as the "Sobukwe clause."

history.q: Who was the first president of the South African Native National Congress, the forerunner of the ANC, founded in 1912?
history.fact: The congress was founded in Bloemfontein on 8 January 1912 and renamed the African National Congress in 1923.

history.q: Which 1913 law restricted Black South Africans' ownership of land to a small share of the country?
history.fact: Sol Plaatje documented its effects in his book "Native Life in South Africa" (1916).

technology.q: Which surgeon performed the world's first human-to-human heart transplant, in Cape Town in 1967?
technology.fact: The operation took place at Groote Schuur Hospital on 3 December 1967; patient Louis Washkansky lived for 18 days.

technology.q: Which Pretoria-born entrepreneur founded the rocket company SpaceX in 2002?
technology.fact: Musk left South Africa at 17, moving first to Canada and then to the United States.

technology.q: Which South African entrepreneur became the first African in space, in 2002?
technology.fact: Shuttleworth flew to the International Space Station aboard a Russian Soyuz and spent nearly ten days in space.

technology.q: Which Linux operating system, from Mark Shuttleworth's company Canonical, takes its name from a Nguni word about shared humanity?
technology.fact: Ubuntu is often summed up as "I am because we are," a philosophy championed by Desmond Tutu.

technology.q: South Africa is the world's largest producer of which precious metal?
technology.fact: The Bushveld Complex north of Pretoria holds most of the world's known reserves of platinum-group metals.

technology.q: The Square Kilometre Array radio telescope is being built in South Africa and which other country?
technology.fact: South Africa hosts the dish antennas in the Karoo, while Australia hosts thousands of low-frequency antennas.

technology.q: Mponeng, one of the deepest mines on Earth at around 4 km down, extracts which metal?
technology.fact: Rock at the bottom of Mponeng is hot enough that ice slurry is pumped down to cool the tunnels for miners.

technology.q: Which record-breaking gem was found at the Premier Mine near Pretoria in 1905?
technology.fact: At 3,106 carats it was cut into several stones, including the Great Star of Africa set in the British royal sceptre.

technology.q: Which diamond company was founded in Kimberley in 1888?
technology.fact: The company took its name from the De Beer brothers, whose farm lay on top of the rich diamond pipes.

technology.q: Which South African company, founded in 1950, became known for making liquid fuels from coal?
technology.fact: Sasol uses the Fischer-Tropsch process, a German method for turning coal-derived gas into fuels and chemicals.

technology.q: What is the name of South Africa's state-owned electricity utility?
technology.fact: Eskom generates the large majority of South Africa's electricity, mostly from coal-fired power stations.

technology.q: Which array of 64 radio dishes in the Karoo was inaugurated in 2018?
technology.fact: MeerKAT produced one of the most detailed radio images of the centre of the Milky Way and will be folded into the SKA.

technology.q: Which Johannesburg-born physicist shared the 1979 Nobel Prize for the theory behind CT scanning?
technology.fact: Cormack did key early work while at the University of Cape Town and Groote Schuur Hospital.

technology.q: The Southern African Large Telescope (SALT) stands near which small Karoo town?
technology.fact: Sutherland's dark, dry skies make it home to many telescopes; it is also one of the coldest towns in the country.

technology.q: Which Pretoria-born scientist won the 1951 Nobel Prize for his work on a yellow fever vaccine?
technology.fact: Theiler's 17D vaccine strain, developed in the 1930s, is still the basis of yellow fever vaccines today.

technology.q: The Kreepy Krauly, invented in South Africa in the 1970s, automatically cleans what?
technology.fact: The suction-powered cleaner creeps along the pool floor and walls and became popular around the world.

technology.q: Which South African-born biologist shared the 2002 Nobel Prize for research using the tiny worm C. elegans?
technology.fact: Brenner, born in Germiston, also helped show that the genetic code is read in three-letter units.

technology.q: Which anatomist described the fossil "Taung Child" as a human ancestor in 1925?
technology.fact: Dart named the species Australopithecus africanus; the skull came from a limestone quarry at Taung.

technology.q: The dolos, an interlocking concrete block used to protect harbour walls, was invented in which city?
technology.fact: The odd H-shaped blocks scatter wave energy and now guard breakwaters and coastlines around the world.

technology.q: Which hominin species was announced in 2015 from fossils found in the Rising Star cave system?
technology.fact: More than 1,500 fossil elements were recovered by a team that included slim "underground astronauts" squeezing through narrow passages.

technology.q: "Little Foot", one of the most complete Australopithecus skeletons ever found, came from which caves?
technology.fact: Freeing Little Foot from rock took about 20 years of painstaking excavation.

technology.q: Which internet security company, founded by Mark Shuttleworth, was sold to VeriSign in 1999?
technology.fact: Thawte issued digital certificates for secure websites; the sale funded Shuttleworth's trip to space.

technology.q: Which South African media company made a famously profitable investment in China's Tencent in 2001?
technology.fact: Naspers paid about US$32 million for its stake, which grew to be worth well over US$100 billion.

technology.q: Koeberg, Africa's first commercial nuclear power station, is near which city?
technology.fact: Koeberg's first reactor began commercial operation in 1984 on the Atlantic coast north of Cape Town.

technology.q: Which palaeontologist found the "Mrs Ples" skull at Sterkfontein in 1947, with John Robinson?
technology.fact: The nickname comes from the skull's original classification as Plesianthropus transvaalensis.

art.q: Which South African singer was known worldwide as "Mama Africa"?
art.fact: Makeba's 1967 hit "Pata Pata" made her one of the first African musicians to top international charts.

art.q: Which a cappella group sang on Paul Simon's 1986 album "Graceland"?
art.fact: Founded by Joseph Shabalala, the group sings isicathamiya, a soft-stepping Zulu choral style.

art.q: Which 2009 science-fiction film by Neill Blomkamp is set in Johannesburg?
art.fact: The film's stranded aliens are nicknamed "prawns"; it earned four Oscar nominations including Best Picture.

art.q: Which South African film won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film in 2006?
art.fact: Directed by Gavin Hood, Tsotsi is based on Athol Fugard's only novel and is set in a Johannesburg township.

art.q: Which hymn, composed by Enoch Sontonga in 1897, forms part of South Africa's national anthem?
art.fact: The anthem blends it with "Die Stem van Suid-Afrika" and is sung in five of the country's languages.

art.q: Which Clint Eastwood film tells the story of the 1995 Rugby World Cup in South Africa?
art.fact: Morgan Freeman played Nelson Mandela and Matt Damon played Springbok captain François Pienaar.

art.q: Which Nobel Prize-winning author wrote the novel "Disgrace" (1999)?
art.fact: Coetzee was the first author to win the Booker Prize twice, and he received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2003.

art.q: Who wrote the 1948 novel "Cry, the Beloved Country"?
art.fact: The novel follows a Zulu pastor searching for his son in Johannesburg and has sold millions of copies.

art.q: Which South African-born actress won the Best Actress Oscar for "Monster" (2003)?
art.fact: Theron grew up on a farm near Benoni, and Afrikaans was her first language.

art.q: Which trumpeter had a US number-one hit with "Grazing in the Grass" in 1968?
art.fact: Masekela also wrote "Bring Him Back Home," which became an anthem of the campaign to free Nelson Mandela.

art.q: Which author of "July's People" won the 1991 Nobel Prize in Literature?
art.fact: Several of Gordimer's books were banned in South Africa during apartheid.

art.q: Which jazz pianist, once known as Dollar Brand, composed the anthem "Mannenberg"?
art.fact: Recorded in 1974 and named after a Cape Flats township, "Mannenberg" became a soundtrack of resistance.

art.q: Which artist makes animated films by repeatedly drawing, erasing and redrawing in charcoal?
art.fact: Kentridge photographs each change to a single drawing, leaving ghostly smudges that become part of the film.

art.q: Which Ndebele artist painted a BMW Art Car in her community's geometric style in 1991?
art.fact: Mahlangu was the first woman to paint a car in BMW's Art Car series, following artists such as Warhol and Lichtenstein.

art.q: Which playwright wrote "'Master Harold'...and the Boys"?
art.fact: Set in a Port Elizabeth tearoom in 1950, the play premiered in the United States in 1982.

art.q: Which musical by Mbongeni Ngema, about students in the 1976 uprising, reached Broadway in 1988?
art.fact: A 1992 film version starred Leleti Khumalo and Whoopi Goldberg, with Miriam Makeba as Sarafina's mother.

art.q: Which South African dance-music genre, known for its deep "log drum" basslines, rose to global fame in the late 2010s?
art.fact: Amapiano, slang for "the pianos," emerged from townships in Gauteng province before spreading worldwide.

art.q: Which author of "The Lord of the Rings" was born in Bloemfontein in 1892?
art.fact: Tolkien left South Africa aged three and grew up in England, but he was born in the Orange Free State's capital.

art.q: Pieces of ochre engraved with cross-hatched lines about 75,000 years ago were found in which cave?
art.fact: Blombos, on the southern Cape coast, also yielded shell beads that are among the oldest known jewellery.

art.q: Which Expressionist painter's former home in Rosebank, Cape Town, is now a museum of her work?
art.fact: Stern lived at The Firs for nearly four decades; the museum also displays her collection of African and world art.

art.q: Which landscape painter created the Station Panels for Johannesburg's railway station in the early 1930s?
art.fact: Pierneef's panels show stylised, flattened scenes of South African landscapes in bold, clean lines.

art.q: Which painter of township street scenes left South Africa for Paris in 1947?
art.fact: Sekoto's "Yellow Houses" (1940) was the first work by a Black artist bought by the Johannesburg Art Gallery.

art.q: Which 1950s magazine chronicled Sophiatown's jazz, fashion and writing, with contributors such as Can Themba?
art.fact: Drum's photographers and writers captured a vibrant township culture before Sophiatown was demolished.

art.q: Which Cape Town museum of contemporary African art opened in 2017 inside a converted grain silo?
art.fact: Architect Thomas Heatherwick carved a cathedral-like atrium out of the silo's concrete tubes.

art.q: Solomon Linda's 1939 Zulu song "Mbube" was later adapted into which famous pop song?
art.fact: "Mbube" means "lion" in Zulu; in 2006 Linda's heirs reached a settlement over royalties for the song.

politics.q: Who was South Africa's first democratically elected president?
politics.fact: Mandela was inaugurated in Pretoria on 10 May 1994 and served a single five-year term.

politics.q: With whom did Nelson Mandela share the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize?
politics.fact: The prize honoured their work for the peaceful end of apartheid and the foundations of a new democracy.

politics.q: South Africa has three capital cities. Which is the seat of the executive branch?
politics.fact: The President's offices are in Pretoria's Union Buildings, designed by Herbert Baker and completed in 1913.

politics.q: How many official languages were recognised in South Africa's 1996 constitution?
politics.fact: They include isiZulu, isiXhosa, Afrikaans, English, Sesotho, Setswana and Xitsonga, among others.

politics.q: Which Afrikaans word, meaning "separateness", names the system of racial segregation enforced from 1948?
politics.fact: Apartheid laws controlled where people could live, work, study and travel according to their racial classification.

politics.q: Which party governed South Africa from 1948 to 1994 and introduced apartheid?
politics.fact: The National Party won the 1948 election, in which most South Africans could not vote.

politics.q: Which party won the most votes in every South African general election from 1994 to 2024?
politics.fact: Founded in 1912, the ANC is one of the oldest liberation movements in Africa.

politics.q: Which body, chaired by Desmond Tutu, heard testimony on human rights violations committed during apartheid?
politics.fact: The TRC could grant amnesty to those who fully disclosed politically motivated crimes; its hearings were broadcast nationwide.

politics.q: Who succeeded Nelson Mandela as President of South Africa in 1999?
politics.fact: Mbeki, who had been Mandela's deputy president, became known for championing the idea of an "African Renaissance."

politics.q: Which city is home to South Africa's Supreme Court of Appeal and known as the judicial capital?
politics.fact: Bloemfontein, "fountain of flowers" in Afrikaans, was once the capital of the Orange Free State.

politics.q: Which prime minister, often called the "architect of apartheid", was assassinated in Parliament in 1966?
politics.fact: Verwoerd was stabbed in the House of Assembly in Cape Town on 6 September 1966 by a parliamentary messenger.

politics.q: In what year did South Africa become a republic?
politics.fact: It left the Commonwealth at the same time and rejoined in 1994 after its first democratic election.

politics.q: In which city does South Africa's Constitutional Court sit?
politics.fact: The court stands on Constitution Hill, a former prison complex where both Gandhi and Mandela were once held.

politics.q: In what year did Nelson Mandela sign South Africa's current constitution into law?
politics.fact: Mandela signed it at Sharpeville on 10 December 1996, and it took effect in February 1997.

politics.q: On 2 February 1990, which president announced the unbanning of the ANC and other liberation movements?
politics.fact: De Klerk made the announcement in his speech at the opening of Parliament; Mandela was released nine days later.

politics.q: Which South African prime minister helped draft the preamble to the United Nations Charter?
politics.fact: Smuts was the only person to sign the founding documents of both the League of Nations and the United Nations.

politics.q: Who became the first prime minister of the Union of South Africa in 1910?
politics.fact: Botha had been a Boer general in the war against Britain only a decade earlier.

politics.q: Which future president was the ANC's chief negotiator during the constitutional talks of the early 1990s?
politics.fact: Ramaphosa had earlier built the National Union of Mineworkers into one of the country's largest trade unions.

politics.q: Which politician led the Inkatha Freedom Party from its founding in 1975 until 2019?
politics.fact: Buthelezi also served as Minister of Home Affairs from 1994 to 2004; he died in 2023 aged 95.

politics.q: Who became the first Speaker of the National Assembly after the 1994 election?
politics.fact: Ginwala served as Speaker for ten years, from 1994 to 2004.

politics.q: Which MP was for 13 years the only Progressive Party member in Parliament, opposing apartheid laws?
politics.fact: Suzman visited prisons, including Robben Island, to check on conditions for political prisoners.

politics.q: Who became the first State President when South Africa became a republic in 1961?
politics.fact: Charles Robberts Swart had previously served as the last Governor-General of the Union of South Africa.

politics.q: Which 1950 apartheid law classified every South African by race?
politics.fact: The Act was repealed in June 1991 as negotiations to end apartheid gathered pace.

politics.q: Which leader of the South African Communist Party was assassinated in April 1993?
politics.fact: Mandela gave a televised address appealing for calm, and a date for the first democratic election was soon set.

politics.q: Which ANC leader led the movement in exile for about three decades after it was banned in 1960?
politics.fact: Johannesburg's main airport, O. R. Tambo International, was named after him in 2006.

current-affairs.q: Which team did South Africa beat in the final of the 2019 Rugby World Cup?
current-affairs.fact: The Springboks won 32-12 in Yokohama, Japan, to claim their third world title.

current-affairs.q: Which team did South Africa beat 12-11 in the final of the 2023 Rugby World Cup in Paris?
current-affairs.fact: The win made South Africa the first nation to lift the Webb Ellis Cup four times.

current-affairs.q: Who captained the Springboks to Rugby World Cup titles in both 2019 and 2023?
current-affairs.fact: In 2019 Kolisi became the first Black captain to lift the Rugby World Cup for South Africa.

current-affairs.q: Which song by Master KG featuring Nomcebo Zikode inspired a worldwide dance challenge in 2020?
current-affairs.fact: Videos of nurses, priests and police dancing to the gospel-house hit spread across dozens of countries during the pandemic.

current-affairs.q: In which South African city was the BRICS summit held in August 2023?
current-affairs.fact: At the summit the bloc invited six more countries to join, including Egypt, Ethiopia and Argentina.

current-affairs.q: Which COVID-19 variant was first reported to the WHO by South African scientists in November 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Genomic surveillance teams in South Africa and Botswana detected the variant and shared their data within days.

current-affairs.q: Who was elected President of South Africa by the National Assembly in June 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Ramaphosa was re-elected by Parliament on 14 June 2024, beginning his second full term.

current-affairs.q: What name was given to the multi-party government formed in South Africa after the May 2024 election?
current-affairs.fact: Ten parties eventually joined the arrangement, echoing the name of Mandela's 1994 unity government.

current-affairs.q: Which team did South Africa beat in the ICC World Test Championship final at Lord's in June 2025?
current-affairs.fact: Aiden Markram's century helped captain Temba Bavuma's side win by five wickets for a first ICC title in 27 years.

current-affairs.q: In November 2025, Johannesburg hosted the first leaders' summit held in Africa by which group?
current-affairs.fact: South Africa held the G20 presidency for 2025 and hosted the leaders' summit on 22-23 November.

current-affairs.q: What happened for the first time since 1994 in South Africa's May 2024 general election?
choices: No party won an outright majority
current-affairs.fact: The ANC finished first with about 40% of the vote, which led to the formation of a multi-party government.

current-affairs.q: Which party, led by former president Jacob Zuma, finished third in the May 2024 general election?
current-affairs.fact: Registered only months before the vote, the party won about 14.6% nationally.

current-affairs.q: Which party leader became Minister of Agriculture in South Africa's government in July 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Steenhuisen, leader of the Democratic Alliance, took the post when the Government of National Unity cabinet was announced.

current-affairs.q: What term do South Africans use for the rotating power cuts that reached record levels in 2023?
current-affairs.fact: Eskom announced cuts in "stages" so households could plan around scheduled blackouts using apps and timetables.

current-affairs.q: Damon Galgut won the 2021 Booker Prize for which novel?
current-affairs.fact: Galgut had been shortlisted twice before; the novel follows a white Pretoria family across four funerals.

current-affairs.q: Which South African singer won the first-ever Grammy for Best African Music Performance, in February 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Tyla won with her amapiano-influenced hit "Water," which also became a viral dance trend.

current-affairs.q: Which international title did South Africa's Zozibini Tunzi win in December 2019?
current-affairs.fact: Tunzi, from the Eastern Cape, became the third South African to be crowned Miss Universe.

current-affairs.q: Cape Town hosted the 2023 World Cup of which sport, the first time the tournament was held in Africa?
current-affairs.fact: Australia won the 2023 Netball World Cup, beating England in the final in Cape Town.

current-affairs.q: Which team beat South Africa in the final of the Women's T20 World Cup in Cape Town in February 2023?
current-affairs.fact: It was the first time a South African senior cricket team, women's or men's, had reached a World Cup final.

current-affairs.q: Severe floods in April 2022 caused heavy loss of life in and around which South African city?
current-affairs.fact: Record rainfall in KwaZulu-Natal destroyed homes, roads and parts of Durban's port.

current-affairs.q: In 2021, the city of Port Elizabeth was officially renamed what?
current-affairs.fact: Gqeberha is the isiXhosa name for the Baakens River area; the city's airport was renamed too.

current-affairs.q: In 2023, which language became South Africa's 12th official language?
current-affairs.fact: President Ramaphosa signed the constitutional amendment in July 2023.

current-affairs.q: Which country did South Africa beat in the final of the Women's Africa Cup of Nations in July 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Banyana Banyana won 2-1 in Rabat to claim their first continental title.

current-affairs.q: Tatjana Schoenmaker won Olympic gold at the Tokyo Games in 2021 in which swimming event?
current-affairs.fact: Schoenmaker set a world record of 2:18.95, winning South Africa's first women's Olympic swimming gold since 1996.

current-affairs.q: Which team beat South Africa in the final of the men's T20 World Cup in June 2024?
current-affairs.fact: India won by seven runs in Barbados in South Africa's first men's World Cup final.

general.q: Which flat-topped mountain overlooks the city of Cape Town?
general.fact: Clouds spilling over its summit are known locally as the "tablecloth."

general.q: Which national park in the northeast is one of Africa's largest game reserves?
general.fact: Kruger covers nearly 20,000 square kilometres, roughly the size of Wales, and is home to all of the "Big Five."

general.q: What is South Africa's currency?
general.fact: The rand takes its name from the Witwatersrand, the gold-rich ridge on which Johannesburg is built.

general.q: In what year did South Africa host the FIFA World Cup, the first held in Africa?
general.fact: The tournament made the droning plastic vuvuzela horn famous around the world.

general.q: What is the nickname of South Africa's national rugby union team?
general.fact: The Springbok name and emblem date back to the national team's 1906-07 tour of Britain.

general.q: Which antelope is South Africa's national animal?
general.fact: Springboks are famous for "pronking": bouncing stiff-legged high into the air with an arched back.

general.q: What is South Africa's largest city by population?
general.fact: Johannesburg is one of the largest cities in the world not built on a river, lake or coastline.

general.q: What is the name of South Africa's popular dried, cured meat snack?
general.fact: Biltong is typically made from beef or game, spiced with coriander and vinegar, then air-dried.

general.q: Which flower is South Africa's national flower?
general.fact: The king protea's flower head can be up to 30 cm across, and the national cricket team is nicknamed the Proteas.

general.q: Which cape is the southernmost point of the African continent?
general.fact: A marker at Cape Agulhas shows the official dividing point between the Atlantic and Indian oceans.

general.q: Which mountain range, called uKhahlamba in isiZulu, runs along the border with Lesotho?
general.fact: The uKhahlamba-Drakensberg Park holds thousands of San rock paintings and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

general.q: Which country is completely surrounded by South Africa?
general.fact: Lesotho is the only independent state lying entirely above 1,000 m in elevation.

general.q: Which baked dish of spiced minced meat topped with an egg custard is a Cape Malay classic?
general.fact: Bobotie is often served with yellow rice and chutney, reflecting the Cape's Indonesian and Malaysian heritage.

general.q: Which Durban street food is curry served inside a hollowed-out loaf of bread?
general.fact: Bunny chow grew out of Durban's Indian community, and is ordered by the quarter, half or full loaf.

general.q: Which is South Africa's longest river, flowing west into the Atlantic Ocean?
general.fact: The river forms part of the border with Namibia and plunges through a granite gorge at Augrabies Falls.

general.q: Which city is home to the "Big Hole", one of the largest hand-dug excavations in the world?
general.fact: Miners dug the Big Hole between 1871 and 1914, recovering about 2,700 kg of diamonds.

general.q: Which language is spoken as a first language by the largest number of South Africans?
general.fact: About a quarter of South Africans speak isiZulu at home, while English is the main language of business and media.

general.q: Which Soweto stadium hosted the 2010 FIFA World Cup final?
general.fact: The stadium's design evokes a calabash, an African gourd pot; Nelson Mandela made his last major public appearance there.

general.q: Which university and wine town, founded in 1679, is South Africa's second-oldest European settlement?
general.fact: Stellenbosch is nicknamed the "City of Oaks" for the trees planted by its founder, Governor Simon van der Stel.

general.q: Which canyon in Mpumalanga is one of the largest on Earth?
general.fact: Its viewpoints include the Three Rondavels, rock formations shaped like traditional round huts.

general.q: The Vredefort Dome, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is the remains of what?
general.fact: Formed about two billion years ago, it is the largest verified impact structure on Earth.

general.q: What was Nelson Mandela's first language?
general.fact: Mandela was born in Mvezo in the Eastern Cape; his Xhosa clan name, Madiba, is still used affectionately.

general.q: Which waterfall in the Drakensberg is often ranked among the tallest in the world?
general.fact: Tugela Falls drops about 948 m in five stages from the Amphitheatre escarpment.

general.q: Which cold ocean current flows north along South Africa's west coast?
general.fact: The cold Benguela keeps the Atlantic side chilly, while the warm Agulhas Current washes the east coast.

general.q: What is the name of the fine-leaved shrubland that dominates the Cape Floral Kingdom?
general.fact: Fynbos is extraordinarily diverse, and most of its thousands of plant species grow nowhere else on Earth.

general.q: Which Cape Town neighbourhood, famous for brightly painted houses, is the historic heart of Cape Malay culture?
